Hand-wrought silver spoon - The Theory of the Leisure Class, Chapter Six: some ten to twenty dollars
Machine-made aluminum spoon - The Theory of the Leisure Class, Chapter Six: some ten to twenty cents

Veblen prices the hand-wrought silver spoon at ten to twenty dollars and the machine-made aluminum spoon at ten to twenty cents, making the silver spoon roughly one hundred times more valuable.

The Island - starting point: about seven millions
The Island - after fifty years: population twenty-eight millions, means of subsistence equal to the support of twenty-one millions

Malthus starts the Island at seven millions; after fifty years (two 25-year periods) the population would be twenty-eight millions while subsistence would support only twenty-one millions.

Yes, force is allowed in the unsafe-bridge case. Mill says that if a public officer or anyone else sees a person attempting to cross a bridge ascertained to be unsafe, and there is no time to warn him of his danger, they may seize him and turn him back (Chapter V, Applications). This is no real infringement of his liberty, because liberty consists in doing what one desires, and he does not desire to fall into the river (Chapter V). However, when there is not a certainty but only a danger of mischief, no one but the person himself can judge the sufficiency of the motive prompting him to incur the risk, so he ought only to be warned (Chapter V). Mill's general principle is that the sole end warranting interference with anyone's liberty is self-protection—power over a member of a civilised community against his will can only be rightfully exercised to prevent harm to others (Chapter I, Introductory). The principle does not apply at all to children, or to persons delirious, or in some state of excitement or absorption incompatible with the full use of the reflecting faculty (Chapter V).

Principal states of modern Europe - doubling period: three or four hundred years, or more
American back settlements - doubling period: fifteen years

Comparison: Europe takes roughly 300–400 years to double versus 15 years in the back settlements, so the American rate was roughly 20–27 times faster (e.g., 300/15 = 20; 400/15 ≈ 27).
About 10–11%: New York city had 202,000 inhabitants in 1830 out of the State's 1,900,000.

The corset is "substantially a mutilation" undergone to lower vitality and render the wearer unfit for work (Chapter Seven). Veblen concedes it impairs the wearer's personal attractions, but this loss is offset by the gain in reputability from her visibly increased expensiveness and infirmity (Chapter Seven). It has fallen into disuse among the richest class because a large leisure class has grown up whose wealth makes any aspersion about enforced manual labor an "idle and harmless calumny," so evidence of honorific leisure is no longer needed (Chapter Seven). It persists among the exceptions—wealthy classes in less industrially advanced countries and recently enriched newcomers—because the latter have not yet shed the plebeian canons of taste from their former lower pecuniary grade (Chapter Seven). More broadly, the corset continues wherever it serves as evidence of honorific leisure by arguing physical disability, especially during the period of "snobbery," the transition from lower to upper pecuniary levels (Chapter Seven).

1st edition (1859) - assumptions: breeds when thirty years old, goes on breeding till ninety years old, bringing forth three pair of young in this interval
1st edition (1859) - result: at the end of the fifth century there would be alive fifteen million elephants, descended from the first pair
6th edition (1872) - assumptions: begins breeding when thirty years old, goes on breeding till ninety years old, bringing forth six young in the interval, and surviving till one hundred years old
6th edition (1872) - result: after a period of from 740 to 750 years there would be nearly nineteen million elephants alive descended from the first pair

Between editions, Darwin changed the number of young from "three pair" to "six young" and added the assumption that elephants survive till one hundred years old; the result changed from fifteen million elephants at the end of the fifth century to nearly nineteen million elephants after 740 to 750 years.

Darwin calls it Malthus's doctrine. According to Malthus's Essay, population, when unchecked, increases in a geometrical ratio, while subsistence increases only in an arithmetical ratio (Chapter 1). As his rule from actual experience, he takes that unchecked population doubles every twenty-five years, citing the United States as an example (Chapter 2).

Mill - On Liberty, Chapter I: When society itself is the tyrant, its means of tyrannising are not restricted to the acts done by the hands of its political functionaries—it can tyrannise over the separate individuals who compose it.

Tocqueville - Democracy in America, Volume 1, Chapter Summary: The most dangerous enemies of the State may be in the possession of no functions at all, especially in republics where party influence is the first of authorities and the strength of many a reader is increased by his exercising no legal power.

Both authors agree that the tyranny of the majority extends beyond the acts of public authorities and officials: Mill stresses society's tyranny over individual thought and life through non-political means, while Tocqueville stresses that the gravest offenders may hold no official functions at all, with party influence acting as an authority outside legal power.

Malthus - rule for unchecked population: doubling every twenty-five years (geometrical ratio)
Tocqueville - US population 1790: 3,929,328 (nearly 4,000,000)
Tocqueville - US population 1830: 12,856,165 (nearly 13,000,000)
Tocqueville - stated growth: population "more than tripled in the space of forty years"
Tocqueville - doubling period he gives: NOT_FOUND

Malthus's rule implies roughly a fourfold increase in fifty years; Tocqueville's figures show the population more than tripled in forty years (12,856,165 ÷ 3,929,328 ≈ 3.3), which is consistent with, and even slightly faster than, a twenty-five-year doubling period. Tocqueville gives no explicit doubling period, only the statement that the population more than tripled in forty years.

[1] On Liberty, Chapter IV - Mill's claim: the feeling of the majority in the United States, to whom any appearance of a more showy or costly style of living than they can hope to rival is disagreeable, operates as a tolerably effectual sumptuary law, and in many parts of the Union it is really difficult for a person with a very large income to find any mode of spending it that will not incur popular disapprobation.

[4] The Theory of the Leisure Class, Chapter Five - Veblen's theory: the accepted standard of expenditure in the community or class largely determines a person's standard of living, directly by commending itself to his common sense as right and good, and indirectly through popular insistence on conformity to the accepted scale of expenditure as a matter of propriety, under pain of disesteem and ostracism.

Mill says majority feeling in the United States acts as a "tolerably effectual sumptuary law," making it difficult for people with very large incomes to spend money showily without incurring popular disapprobation. Veblen's theory explains the motive being restrained as the drive toward conspicuous, costly expenditure beyond the accepted community standard, which society polices through disesteem and ostracism.
